A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, methods, and principal experiments. All 31 pages of v2 and 35 pages of v3, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures supporting reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original agent simulations, attack and defense searches, transfer experiments, ablations, and helpfulness evaluations, including Tables 1–11 and Figures 3–5.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds a live-Outlook case study and detailed search outcomes in Tables 12–16.

M1.justification: The ReAct agents, alternating attack/defense search, parallel attack threads, and cross-thread propagation remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–2 and optimizer prompts match; the added search histories document existing procedures rather than introduce a new method.

E1.justification: Training-5 and Testing-100 remain the simulation datasets. Section 4.3.2 adds a mental-health information extraction scenario using a live Outlook account and screenshot-based browser interaction, extending evaluation beyond the mock application environments.

E2.justification: Tables 1–11, Figure 4, and Appendix L retain the same backbone comparisons, search alternatives, and directly generated defense comparator. The new browser case study adds no comparative baseline; newly cited DSPy is not evaluated.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the stated Gemini Flash leakage detector from a 1,024-token thinking budget to non-thinking mode. The new case study also introduces GPT-5.1 through ChatGPT Atlas and screenshot-based testing. The PDFs do not establish that the retained simulations were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds a small simulation-to-real transfer case study and Appendix O's examination of successful and unsuccessful search iterations, supported by Tables 12–16. Existing ablations, model-behavior analyses, search-consistency checks, and helpfulness analysis are retained.

E5.justification: The new browser case study explicitly reports five trials. Existing simulation repeat counts, the two independent search runs, and Table 5's 95% bootstrap confidence intervals using 10,000 resamples remain unchanged; this is not an increase in runs for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: The new Outlook attack succeeds in three of five trials; the other two flag suspicious consent. Tables 12–16 add instruction-level search outcomes, including LV 0.92 at step 8 of the illustrated A2 search. Existing Tables 1–11 and result plots retain their values.

T1.justification: The leak-velocity and leak-score definitions, mathematical search formulation, and algorithmic expressions are unchanged. Neither version adds or removes theoretical propositions, proofs, or formal guarantees.

C1.justification: The abstract moderates the practical implication from 'demonstrating strong practical utility' to 'providing useful insights' for developing privacy-aware agents. The central contributions concerning automated risk discovery, alternating search, and transfer remain intact.

C2.justification: v3 removes v2's explicit limitations discussion covering computational constraints, changing model vulnerabilities, and deployment safeguards or human oversight. It adds a cautiously qualified interpretation of real-world transfer and explains unsuccessful search iterations through execution difficulty or contextual ineffectiveness in Appendix O.

D1.justification: v3 supplies intermediate instructions, documents the illustrated D1 search stopping at step 5 after reaching zero LV, and adds an inventory of supplemental configurations, code, and trajectories. The code/data link is retained. The inventory's 'Training-100' conflicts with Training-5 in Section 4.2 and does not establish expanded training coverage.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to Romera-Paredes et al. on program search, Novikov et al. on AlphaEvolve, and Khattab et al. on DSPy. Section 2 adds a focused distinction between sparse feedback in vulnerability discovery and feedback from ordinary task-performance optimization.

P1.justification: Most prose and section organization are retained. Local changes include the conference-publication header, abstract edits, an expanded related-work paragraph, the case-study paragraph, a reproducibility statement replacing the limitations section, and a new appendix labeled O without a descriptive title.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 12–16 presenting search steps, instructions, and leak velocities. Existing Figures 1–17 and Tables 1–11 retain their designs, with appendix reflow and relocation, including Figure 17 sharing a page with the new Table 13.

improvement.justification: The live-Outlook case study adds preliminary evidence beyond v2's simulations, while Tables 12–16 make successful and failed search iterations easier to inspect. These modestly improve empirical grounding and transparency. The gains are tempered by the small case-study scope, removal of the broader limitations discussion, and the inconsistent 'Training-100' disclosure; the core method and main results remain stable.
